title: Greece versus France: a debt ranking tells only half the story
seoTitle: Greece vs France: debt levels and debt direction are not the same
summary: Greece has the higher debt ratio, but a ranking alone misses the direction of travel. A fair comparison separates the starting burden, the change and the cost of financing it.
excerpt: A debt league table shows position, not progress. Greece and France illustrate why both matter before you draw a conclusion about public finances.

body:
Put Greece and France into a European debt ranking and Greece looks worse. Ask which country reduced its debt burden over the previous year and the answer changes. Both observations can be correct. The mistake is to treat a position in the table as a verdict on progress.

For anyone trying to understand Europe’s public finances, this distinction matters more than another dramatic debt milestone. A country can make substantial progress and still carry a very heavy burden. Another can start lower and move in the wrong direction.

Compare the same quarter before comparing the countries

Eurostat’s provisional release of 21 July put Greek government debt at 143.5% of GDP at the end of Q1 2026, down from 152.9% a year earlier. France stood at 117.6%, up from 113.6% in the same comparison.

These are deliberately figures from one release, using one definition and one reference quarter. They are not presented as the latest national readings available in October. Later publications can revise an earlier quarter as well as add a new one.

The distinction is especially important when a national statistical office publishes before the next European comparison. Combining one country’s fresh observation with another country’s older figure can make a league table look current without making it comparable.

The level and the change answer different questions

On that common basis, Greece’s ratio was higher. It had also fallen by 9.4 percentage points over a year, while France’s had risen by 4.0 points. Those differences are percentage points, not percentage changes in the amount owed.

The level describes the size of debt relative to annual economic output. The change shows whether that relationship has improved or worsened over a stated period. Neither tells you, on its own, exactly why it moved or what will happen next.

On our European debt-to-GDP comparison, start with the level, then check the period and recent history. Treat the ranking as the beginning of a question, not its answer. The country at the top has not necessarily made the worst recent decisions.

A falling burden can still be the larger burden

Consider two fictional countries. One begins with debt equal to 150% of its economy and reduces the ratio by five percentage points. The other starts at 110% and adds three points. Their new ratios are 145% and 113%.

The first improved. It is still much more indebted on this measure. The second deteriorated. It still has the lower ratio. There is no contradiction, and there is no basis here for predicting when the two might cross. Extending one year’s changes indefinitely would turn an illustration into an unsupported forecast.

This is also why a falling ratio is not the same thing as repayment. The economy measured in money can grow faster than debt. To establish what happened to borrowing itself, you need the debt amounts and the financial accounts as well.

Progress is not a credit rating

It would be tempting to turn the comparison around and declare Greece safer because its direction looked better. That would repeat the same mistake in reverse. A recent improvement does not erase an accumulated burden or settle the terms on which it must be financed.

The European Commission’s Debt Sustainability Monitor examines risks over several horizons and considers additional factors. Its framework is useful precisely because a single ratio cannot describe every financing risk. The report cited here uses older forecast assumptions; it is not an October assessment of either country.

Questions about interest costs, repayment schedules and future budget balances belong beside the ranking. They require their own evidence. A numerical gap between two ratios is not a measured probability of default, nor a countdown to one.

What would count as convincing improvement?

Look for a sustained change across comparable observations, then investigate its causes. Did debt rise more slowly? Did the economy expand? Were temporary financial transactions important? A favourable quarter deserves attention, but it cannot establish that a government has solved a long-running problem.

The Greece country page and the France country page let you inspect each trajectory and its reference period. A moving modelled counter should not be confused with another official quarterly observation. Compare like with like before interpreting the difference.

Eurostat scheduled its next debt release for 21 October. The useful task is to reassess both countries on the newly published common basis, including revisions, rather than attach a new date to an old comparison. This article does not anticipate those results.

Greece’s higher ratio describes the burden it still carries. A falling ratio describes progress against that burden. France’s lower starting position does not cancel a rising trend. Read all three statements together, and a league table becomes a tool for understanding rather than a shortcut to the wrong conclusion.
